Start with the question, unit and sample: A small example separates a sample from the population. Suppose a town wants the average weekly energy bill for all 10,000 households, but first calculates the mean from five bills: £40, £50, £60, £70 and £80. Their sample mean is (£40 + £50 + £60 + £70 + £80) ÷ 5 = £60 per week. That £60 describes those five households and is an estimate of the town-wide average—not a fact about every household. A larger sample can make random error smaller, but it still needs a sensible route into the sample.

Ask how the five households were chosen. A random sample drawn from a complete household list can support a town-wide description under its design; five online volunteers may not, even if their arithmetic is perfect. Random sampling helps decide whom the evidence represents. Random assignment instead decides who receives a programme and can support a causal comparison. They solve different problems. See “Penn State STAT 200 — Descriptive Statistics” in the linked sources for a fuller introduction.

Suppose a researcher asks, ‘What was the typical monthly transport cost per household in March 2026?’ The unit is pounds per household per month, not pounds per person. In an illustrative synthetic sample of four households, costs are £90, £110, £130 and £170, so the sample mean is (£90 + £110 + £130 + £170) ÷ 4 = £500 ÷ 4 = £125 per household per month. This statistic describes the sampled households; it does not establish the population mean if renters, rural households or nonrespondents were missed. A sampling frame should define eligible households and the date window before collection. Random sampling can support generalization, but it cannot remove measurement error or guarantee a causal interpretation. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 1: Introduction to Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.
Match variable type to a useful display: Illustrative synthetic example (January–June 2025): a local economic office records one weekly grocery bill for each of 12 households, in pounds, and each household’s tenancy type. Grocery spending is quantitative, so group the bills into £40–59 (4 households), £60–79 (5), and £80–99 (3), then draw a histogram with spending in pounds on the horizontal axis and household count on the vertical axis. The five households in the middle bin represent 5 ÷ 12 = 41.7% of this small sample. Tenancy type is categorical, so show its counts or proportions in a bar chart rather than placing labels on a numerical axis. The displays describe this six-month snapshot; they do not turn the categories into measured quantities.

A histogram or bar chart can reveal concentration, skew or group composition in the recorded sample, but it cannot establish that tenancy type causes higher grocery spending, nor that these 12 households represent every household in the area. Before choosing a display, check that each row refers to the same time unit and household, that pounds are defined consistently, and that the denominator for every proportion is stated; if bills are repeated weekly observations, account for that dependence rather than treating them as 12 independent households. Do not read a histogram bar’s height as a probability unless it has been normalized and the bin widths are comparable. The linked source “NIST/SEMATECH — Histogram and exploratory data analysis” gives further guidance.

Imagine an illustrative synthetic survey of 20 small businesses recording payment method and invoice amount in euros. Payment method has counts: bank transfer 12, card 5 and cash 3; the proportions are 12 ÷ 20 = 60%, 5 ÷ 20 = 25% and 3 ÷ 20 = 15%, so a bar chart suits the categories. Invoice amount is quantitative: if six selected invoices are €40, €40, €60, €80, €80 and €200, a dot plot makes the repeated €40 and €80 values visible, while a histogram can show the long right tail. These displays summarize the recorded invoices, not all businesses. The €200 value may be genuine, so do not delete it merely to make the chart symmetrical. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST/SEMATECH — Histogram and exploratory data analysis’ in the linked sources.
Compare center and spread with a worked: For an illustrative synthetic set of five weekly sales changes, measured in percent, use −2%, 0%, 1%, 1% and 10%. The mean is (−2 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 10) ÷ 5 = 10 ÷ 5 = 2%, while the median is 1% after ordering the values. The range is 10% − (−2%) = 12 percentage points, showing the total span. Here, the 10% week raises the mean above four of the five observations, so the median may better represent a typical week. However, the median can hide how far an extreme lies from the rest, and the range depends on two observations. These summaries describe sales changes; they do not explain why the 10% week occurred or prove a promotion caused it. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 2: Summarizing Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.
Use quantiles and robust summaries: Consider eight illustrative synthetic delivery times in minutes, already ordered: 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 45 and 50. Using the median-of-halves convention, the median is (16 + 18) ÷ 2 = 17 minutes. The lower half gives Q1 = (14 + 15) ÷ 2 = 14.5 minutes, and the upper half gives Q3 = (20 + 45) ÷ 2 = 32.5 minutes. Therefore IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 32.5 − 14.5 = 18 minutes, describing the middle 50% under this convention. The 45- and 50-minute deliveries make the distribution right-skewed, so the median and IQR may communicate a typical delivery better than the mean and standard deviation. Quantiles are not guarantees about future maximum delays, and another interpolation rule may give slightly different values. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 2: Summarizing Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.
Transform levels into meaningful changes: Suppose an illustrative synthetic asset has prices of $80 at Monday’s close, $84 on Tuesday and $81 on Wednesday. Tuesday’s simple return is 84 ÷ 80 − 1 = 0.05 = 5%, while Wednesday’s is 81 ÷ 84 − 1 = −0.035714..., or about −3.57%; the denominator changes because each return uses the prior day’s price. If a quoted interest rate moves from 4.20% to 4.65%, the change is 0.45 percentage points, not 0.45%: the relative increase is 0.45 ÷ 4.20 ≈ 10.7%. A two-day price change can be computed from 81 ÷ 80 − 1 = 1.25%, but it hides the interim rise and fall. These transformations describe movement, not its cause or a reliable forecast. For a fuller treatment, see ‘FRED — What is FRED?’ in the linked sources.
Communicate uncertainty and practical im: Suppose an illustrative synthetic sample estimates an average monthly fee difference of $3.00 between two customer groups, with a 95% confidence interval from −$1.00 to $7.00 per customer per month. The interval’s width is $7 − (−1) = $8, so the estimate is not precise enough to rule out no difference or a modest negative difference under the stated method. If a business has pre-specified $10 per month as the threshold worth acting on, even the upper endpoint, $7, is below that practical threshold. A large sample could narrow the interval without making a $3 difference economically important; conversely, a small sample could leave a meaningful effect uncertain. This interval does not prove group membership causes fees, especially without random assignment. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 200 — Descriptive Statistics’ in the linked sources.

Conditioning changes the reference group: Read the phrase after the vertical bar as the group you have kept. In an illustrative set of 200 days, event B occurs on 50 days; event A occurs on 30 of those B days. So P(A|B) = 30 ÷ 50 = 60%: among B days, 60% also had A. If A happened on 80 of all 200 days, its overall rate is P(A) = 80 ÷ 200 = 40%. The conditional rate is higher in this sample, but that comparison by itself does not explain why.

Now reverse the question: P(B|A) = 30 ÷ 80 = 37.5%, not 60%, because the reference group is now the 80 A days. A quick check is to write the denominator in words before calculating: “out of the B days” or “out of the A days.” This prevents the common mistake of swapping P(A|B) with P(B|A). If the question is about a rare warning, also include the event’s base rate and false alarms; the MIT OpenCourseWare probability notes linked below develop these conditional-probability ideas.

Conditioning is a denominator choice, so write the reference group in words before calculating. In a synthetic survey of 400 illustrative households, 160 rent, and 48 renters report cutting food spending; among 240 homeowners, 36 report the same action. The conditional rates are 48/160=30% for renters and 36/240=15% for homeowners. The difference is 15 percentage points, not 15 percent: 30%−15%=15 percentage points. It describes an association within this sample, measured over the survey’s stated month; it does not show renting caused the spending change. Nonresponse or different interpretations of “cutting” could distort both rates. For a fuller treatment, see “MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05 — Probability and Statistics” in the linked sources.
Define events, outcomes and horizons: Illustrative example: consider 120 synthetic county-month observations from January 2016 through December 2025. Let event A mean that the county unemployment rate was above 6% in a month, and event B mean that the share of households behind on rent was above 10% in that same month. Suppose A occurred in 36 months, B in 30 months, and both occurred together in 18 months. Then P(A) = 36 ÷ 120 = 0.30, or 30%; P(B) = 30 ÷ 120 = 0.25, or 25%; and P(A and B) = 18 ÷ 120 = 0.15, or 15%. The union, meaning at least one event, is P(A or B) = (36 + 30 − 18) ÷ 120 = 48 ÷ 120 = 40%. These are monthly frequencies for this defined county-period, not claims about every place or future month.

This calculation describes how often the two defined conditions appeared in the synthetic county-month record; it cannot establish that high unemployment caused rent arrears, or that the same percentages will hold in another region, season, or economic regime. A key check is to confirm that every month uses the same unemployment and rent-arrears definitions, covers the same county, and has no duplicated or missing month silently changing the denominator. Also decide whether the observations are genuinely comparable before treating their frequency as informative. Do not read P(A and B) = 15% as “15% of high-unemployment months had arrears”; that would require P(B|A), whose denominator is the 36 A months. In the linked sources below, “MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05 — Probability and Statistics” develops the event and probability framework.

An event can be defined at several levels, and the unit determines the denominator. Suppose an illustrative synthetic retailer records 50 store-weeks: 12 store-weeks have a stockout, and 5 of those also have a delivery delay. Then P(stockout)=12/50=0.24, or 24% of store-weeks, while P(both)=5/50=0.10, or 10% of store-weeks. If the question instead asks for the share of stockouts with delays, the denominator is 12: 5/12=0.4167, or 41.67%. These are weekly store-level frequencies, not percentages of annual sales or evidence that delays caused stockouts. Definitions must keep the same store-week unit and period; mixing daily records with weekly records changes the experiment. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 3: Probability (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.
Update base rates with Bayes' rule: Bayes’ rule is especially useful when a screening signal is uncommon but imperfect. Consider 2,000 synthetic, illustrative loan applications: 4% are assumed to need review, so 0.04×2,000=80 cases. A model flags 75% of those (0.75×80=60) and falsely flags 8% of the remaining 1,920, giving 0.08×1,920=153.6, or about 154 false flags. The approximate positive predictive value is 60/(60+154)=60/214≈28.0%. Thus most flags are not confirmed cases, despite 75% sensitivity. Rounding and the assumed base rate affect the result; the calculation is not evidence that the model causes approval outcomes or that the rates persist in another population. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 3: Probability (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.
Separate independence, correlation and c: A small correlation can conceal dependence when variables move together only in particular states. Take four synthetic quarterly observations of an index return X and a commodity return Y, measured in percentage points: (−2,−1), (−1,−2), (1,2), (2,1). Their means are both 0 percentage points, and the products XY are 2, 2, 2, and 2, so the sample covariance is positive rather than zero, even though the pairs do not line up perfectly. A different nonlinear pattern could have zero linear correlation while still changing systematically. This tiny illustration is not a reliable estimate of economic dependence; four quarters cannot establish stability, and association cannot identify causality. For a fuller treatment, see “MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05 — Probability and Statistics” in the linked sources.
From expected value to portfolio varianc: Expected return and variance answer different questions: one is a weighted average in percent, the other measures squared percentage-point dispersion. Suppose a synthetic two-asset portfolio puts 75% in an asset with expected one-month return 2% and 25% in an asset with expected return −1%. Its expected return is 0.75×2%+0.25×(−1%)=1.50%−0.25%=1.25% for one month. This is an average under the stated probabilities, not a guaranteed 1.25% cash gain. If the weights sum to 100%, the interpretation is a fully invested portfolio; fees, rebalancing and changing covariances are omitted. The result also does not establish that either asset caused the portfolio outcome. For a fuller treatment, see “CFA Institute — Measuring and Managing Market Risk” in the linked sources.
Quantiles, VaR and tail uncertainty: Quantiles depend on the loss unit, horizon and tail convention. Suppose five synthetic one-week losses, already sorted and measured as percentages of portfolio value, are 0%, 1%, 2%, 6% and 9%. If we define the worst 20% as the single largest observation, the tail-average loss is 9%. This finite-sample convention is sensitive to sample size; another empirical quantile rule can give a different 80th-percentile cutoff. The remaining four weeks do not tell us how large a rarer loss could be. This toy calculation is sensitive to sample size and interpolation choices, and weekly losses may be dependent, so it is not a maximum-loss guarantee or a forecast. For a fuller treatment, see “CFA Institute — Measuring and Managing Market Risk” in the linked sources.

What the central limit theorem actually: Keep two pictures separate: the spread of individual observations and the spread of averages from repeated samples. For a teaching example, suppose household weekly energy bills have a standard deviation of about £200. A random sample of 100 households has a standard error for its average of roughly £200 ÷ √100 = £20. If we repeatedly took new samples of 100 from the same population, their averages would vary around the true average; they would not all equal it. With 400 independent households, the standard error would be about £200 ÷ √400 = £10.

The central limit theorem helps explain why that repeated-sample distribution of averages can look approximately bell-shaped under suitable conditions. It does not say that individual bills become bell-shaped, nor that a large sample repairs a biased survey. The shortcut relies on an appropriate sampling process and enough effectively independent information; strong clustering, serial dependence, very heavy tails or a changing population can alter the approximation. See the Penn State STAT 200 notes on Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem linked below.

The CLT is especially useful when the raw observations are uneven but the average combines enough suitable observations. In an illustrative synthetic model, weekly claims have mean $300 and standard deviation $80 per household-week. For n = 16 independent households, SE(x̄) ≈ $80 ÷ √16 = $80 ÷ 4 = $20 per household-week. For n = 64, SE(x̄) ≈ $80 ÷ 8 = $10 per household-week, so the typical sampling spread halves when the sample quadruples. This describes repeated sample averages, not individual claims becoming normal; a particular sample can still be unusual. Independence, a stable population, and finite, well-behaved variance matter. Clustering households or extreme tails can make the simple calculation too optimistic. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Central Limit Theorem” in the linked sources.
Standard error and an interval in percen: Illustrative synthetic example — A regional labour economist estimates the mean district-level unemployment rate in April 2026 from a simple random sample of 64 districts. The sample mean is 6.0%, and the sample standard deviation across districts is 1.6 percentage points. First estimate the standard error of the mean: 1.6 ÷ √64 = 1.6 ÷ 8 = 0.2 percentage points. Using a rough 95% multiplier of 2 gives 6.0% ± 2(0.2 percentage points), or an interval from 5.6% to 6.4%. In this teaching calculation, 6.0% is the sample estimate; the interval expresses sampling uncertainty about the region’s April mean district rate under the stated design, not the rate in any one district or a forecast for May.

The interval method can quantify sampling uncertainty for the stated district-level average, but it cannot repair nonresponse, a biased district list, measurement errors, or a change in labour-market conditions after April; it also does not establish that a policy caused unemployment to change. Check that the 64 districts were sampled in a defensible way, that rates use consistent definitions, and whether spatial clustering or other dependence makes 64 observations fewer than 64 independent pieces of information. Avoid saying there is a 95% probability that this fixed interval contains the mean: the approximately 95% claim belongs to the long-run procedure when its assumptions hold. For the formal sampling-distribution logic, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Sampling Distributions” in the linked sources below.

Standard error is measured in the same units as the estimate, while a percentage-point interval should not be confused with a percent change. Suppose an illustrative synthetic survey of n = 25 stores finds a mean monthly revenue growth of 4% and sample standard deviation 5 percentage points. The estimated standard error is 5 ÷ √25 = 5 ÷ 5 = 1 percentage point per month. A rough 95% interval is 4% ± 2(1 percentage point), giving 2% to 6% monthly growth. The half-width is 2 percentage points, not “2 percent of 4%.” This interval describes uncertainty in the population mean monthly growth under the sampling design; it is not a forecast for next month. Nonresponse, dependence among stores, or changing conditions can invalidate the coverage claim. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Sampling Distributions” in the linked sources.
Four distributions hiding in one finance: A useful way to separate the four objects is to track a question about hourly wages. Suppose a firm’s target population is all 2,000 employees, measured in dollars per hour during March 2026 (illustrative synthetic data). A randomly selected sample of 50 employees is the observed subset. If their wages sum to $1,250 per hour, the sample statistic is x̄ = $1,250 ÷ 50 = $25 per hour. Now imagine repeating that selection many times: the resulting list of sample means is a sampling distribution, also measured in dollars per hour. The population distribution contains individual wages, not sample means. A sample mean estimates a population mean but can differ because of selection noise. It does not describe wage causation or guarantee representativeness. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Sampling Distributions” in the linked sources.
The law of large numbers: stability, not: The law of large numbers concerns the cumulative average, not a promise about each observation. Imagine illustrative synthetic hourly exchange-rate changes of +2%, −1%, +3%, −2%, and +1%. After two observations, the mean is (2 − 1)% ÷ 2 = 0.5% per hour; after five, it is (2 − 1 + 3 − 2 + 1)% ÷ 5 = 0.6% per hour. Adding one new observation can still move the average substantially when n is small. With a stable population and an appropriate sampling process, additional observations tend to reduce this random movement. The result does not remove a systematic sampling bias, serial dependence, or a regime change, and it does not say the next hourly change will be near 0.6%. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 4: Distributions (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.
Bootstrap the statistic, not the story: Bootstrap calculation is transparent when each resample keeps the original sample size and allows repeats. Take an illustrative synthetic sample of four delivery times in minutes: 20, 30, 40, and 50. One bootstrap resample could be 20, 20, 40, 50, whose mean is (20 + 20 + 40 + 50) ÷ 4 = 32.5 minutes. Another could be 30, 30, 50, 50, with mean 40 minutes. Repeating this many times gives a distribution of bootstrap means; its spread approximates uncertainty about the original sample mean, in minutes. It is conditional on the observed four times: an unobserved 90-minute disruption cannot appear unless represented in the data. Ordinary resampling also assumes exchangeable observations, so daily dependence or changing traffic regimes requires caution. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 4: Distributions (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.
From a distribution to a responsible con: A responsible conclusion links the statistic to a clearly stated estimand and avoids jumping from association to cause. Suppose an illustrative synthetic comparison finds average annual returns of 6% for Fund A and 4% for Fund B over 10 years: the arithmetic difference is 6% − 4% = 2 percentage points per year. That comparison does not show Fund A caused the extra return; sector mix, fees, risk, and selection may differ. Nor does a 2-percentage-point average establish that every future year will be better. Report the observation period, currency or return unit, sample construction, uncertainty, and tail behavior. Practical importance also matters: a 2-point gain may be outweighed by a 10-point loss in a rare year. For a fuller treatment, see “MIT OpenCourseWare — Random Walks and Financial Data” in the linked sources.

Build an interval from an estimate and i: Work through the arithmetic in the units of the question. Suppose a representative sample of 100 rented homes has average weekly rent £820 and sample standard deviation £200. The estimated standard error is £200 ÷ √100 = £20. Using 1.96 as a rough 95% multiplier gives £820 ± 1.96 × £20, or about £780.80 to £859.20 per week. The interval is wider when observations vary more and narrower when the sample gives more independent information; it is not a range containing 95% of individual rents.

The coverage interpretation concerns a procedure: if we repeatedly drew suitable samples and built intervals this way, about 95% would cover the fixed population mean under the method’s assumptions. It does not mean there is a 95% probability that this already-calculated interval contains that fixed mean, and it is not a forecast of next week’s rent. Sampling uncertainty also does not automatically include nonresponse, measurement error or a poorly defined population. For formal interval construction and its assumptions, see “NIST — Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals” in the linked sources.

To construct an interval, keep the margin of error in the estimate’s units. Suppose a synthetic survey estimates average monthly transit spending at $64 per commuter, with SE = $5 and a chosen critical value of 2.1. The margin of error is 2.1 × $5 = $10.50, so the interval is $64 − $10.50 = $53.50 to $64 + $10.50 = $74.50 per commuter per month. This range describes uncertainty about the population mean under the sampling model, not the range of individual commuters’ spending. The calculation assumes the sample design and reference distribution are suitable; dependence, nonresponse, or measurement errors may widen actual uncertainty. It also does not establish what a fare change would cause. For a fuller treatment, see “NIST — Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals” in the linked sources.
Bias, variance and mean squared error: Illustrative synthetic example (January–December 2025): suppose a regional economist wants the population mean monthly electricity bill for all households, and the teaching simulation sets that target at £120 per household per month. Across repeated samples, estimator A has average error £0 and standard deviation £15, so its bias is £0 and its variance is 15² = 225 (£/month)²; its mean squared error is 225 + 0² = 225 (£/month)². Estimator B comes from a survey that under-reports bills by £5 on average, with standard deviation £8: its bias is −£5, variance is 8² = 64, and MSE is 64 + (−5)² = 89 (£/month)². B is systematically low but has lower overall squared error in this constructed comparison.

MSE can compare an estimator’s repeated-sampling performance, but it cannot establish that one estimate is correct, that the target was measured without error, or that a survey represents every household. The calculation assumes that the stated target, sampling process and error summaries are meaningful and reasonably stable over the period. Check the sampling frame against the intended household population, inspect missing or under-reported bills, and run a sensitivity analysis for plausible bias values before choosing an estimator. Do not misinterpret lower MSE as proof that an estimator is unbiased or universally best; the loss function and decision purpose matter. For the formal point-estimation framework, see “Penn State STAT 415 — Point Estimation” in the linked sources below.

The bias–variance trade-off becomes clearer when errors have the same units as the target. Imagine two synthetic estimators of mean weekly grocery spending, measured in dollars per household. Estimator A has bias $0 and standard deviation $14, so its variance is 14² = 196 dollars² and its MSE is 196 + 0² = 196 dollars². Estimator B underestimates by $3 on average and has standard deviation $8: variance = 8² = 64 dollars², and MSE = 64 + (−3)² = 73 dollars². B has lower MSE despite systematic error. This conclusion depends on the stated repeated-sampling summaries and the chosen squared-error loss; it does not prove B is best for every decision or population. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 415 — Point Estimation” in the linked sources.
Name the target before calculating: A useful way to make an estimand concrete is to write a measurement statement before collecting data: “mean electricity cost per household per month, in euros, for residents of City A during January–June 2026.” Suppose a synthetic pilot records €92, €108, and €100 for three households. The sample-mean calculation is (€92 + €108 + €100) ÷ 3 = €300 ÷ 3 = €100 per household per month. Here, €100 is the estimate; the citywide six-month mean is the parameter, and “add the observations and divide by sample size” is the estimator. The result does not describe annual cost or other cities, and a volunteer sample may miss households without easy online access. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 415 — Point Estimation” in the linked sources.
Measure sampling variability with standa: Standard error is measured in the same units as the estimate, which helps distinguish it from variance. Consider a synthetic sample of 36 delivery times measured in minutes, with sample standard deviation s = 12 minutes. Since √36 = 6, the estimated standard error of the mean is 12 minutes ÷ 6 = 2 minutes. If the sample size rose to 144 while the spread stayed 12 minutes, SE would be 12 ÷ 12 = 1 minute, so four times as many observations would halve the uncertainty from 2 to 1 minute. This comparison assumes observations contribute roughly independent information and that the sample standard deviation represents the target process. It does not correct biased recruitment, clustered routes, or a changing delivery system. For a fuller treatment, see “NIST — Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals” in the linked sources.
Interpret 95% confidence without a proba: A helpful thought experiment separates the fixed parameter from intervals that change. Suppose a synthetic process has a true mean waiting time of 10 minutes. Five repeated samples produce intervals [9.2, 10.8], [9.6, 10.4], [10.1, 11.3], [8.7, 9.9], and [9.8, 10.6] minutes. Four of these five intervals contain 10 minutes, while the fourth does not: 4 ÷ 5 = 0.80, or 80% in this tiny illustration. A 95% method would approach 95% coverage only across many repetitions, not necessarily five. The example uses a fixed target and synthetic numbers; it does not mean the current interval has a 95% probability of coverage or that future waits will lie inside it. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 7: Inference for Numerical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.
Read intervals for precision, importance: Read an interval against a practical threshold, not only against zero. Suppose a synthetic evaluation estimates that a reminder lowers monthly late fees by 1.2 percentage points, with a 95% interval from 0.2 to 2.2 percentage points. If a reduction of at least 1.0 percentage point is the pre-specified meaningful threshold, the estimate exceeds it, but the interval includes values below it (0.2 and 0.8) as well as above it. Thus the data are compatible with a statistically positive but practically small reduction, or a meaningful one; more precision would help. The calculation concerns an association unless assignment and design support causality, and it does not guarantee the same effect in another population or month. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 7: Inference for Numerical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.

Compute and interpret a p-value: Suppose an illustrative employment programme is estimated to raise an employment rate by 2.4 percentage points, with a standard error of 1.2 percentage points. If the null model says the effect is zero, the estimate is 2.4 ÷ 1.2 = 2 standard errors from zero. A two-sided p-value is the probability, assuming that null model and the test’s assumptions, of getting a test statistic at least this far from zero in either direction; a value near 0.046 is one possible result. The steps are: state the null, calculate the estimate’s distance from it in standard-error units, then measure how much of the null reference distribution is at least as extreme.

That 0.046 is not a 4.6% chance that the programme has no effect, and it says nothing by itself about whether a 2.4-point change is worth the cost. The interpretation also depends on the design, model and analysis being reported. If researchers tried many outcomes or specifications and show only the smallest p-value, the single-test calculation hides the search. Report the estimate, units, interval, design and analysis choices together. The ASA statement and NIST interpretation guide linked below explain why a threshold such as 0.05 is not a verdict.

The tail calculation becomes clearer when the statistic is treated as a distance, not a score for truth. Illustrative synthetic example: an estimated change in a default rate is −1.5 percentage points, with a standard error of 0.75 percentage points, under a zero-change null. Then t = (−1.5 − 0) / 0.75 = −2.0; for a two-sided test, both tails count, so the p-value is approximately 0.046 under a normal reference distribution. This says that results at least 2 standard errors from zero would occur about 4.6% of the time if the model were correct. It does not establish a causal reduction or account for unreported analyses. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.
Read intervals and effect size together: Illustrative synthetic example — Suppose a randomly assigned job-search support programme is evaluated using participants’ annual earnings 12 months after enrolment. The estimated difference between the offered and comparison groups is £600 per worker per year, with a standard error of £250. Relative to a zero-effect null, the test statistic is 600 ÷ 250 = 2.4, giving an approximate two-sided normal p-value of 0.016. A rough 95% interval is £600 ± 1.96 × £250, or about £110 to £1,090 per worker per year. The estimate is positive and the interval excludes zero, but it spans effects below and above a pre-specified practical benchmark of £500 per year. Thus the data are fairly incompatible with zero under this model, while the programme’s economically meaningful size remains uncertain.

An interval and p-value can describe sampling evidence and precision; they cannot alone establish that the programme caused the earnings difference, that the effect lasts beyond 12 months, or that benefits exceed delivery costs. A key check is whether assignment was genuinely random and whether attrition, clustering by training centre, or unequal follow-up could change the standard error or comparison; compare results with reasonable design-appropriate analyses. Avoid saying that p = 0.016 means a 1.6% chance the null is true, or that the interval has a 95% probability of containing the fixed effect. The “American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values” and “NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values” in the linked sources below explain these cautions.

A useful habit is to compare an interval with a decision-relevant benchmark in the same units. Illustrative synthetic example: a policy estimate is an additional 18 minutes of weekly exercise per participant, with a standard error of 10 minutes. An approximate 95% interval is 18 ± 1.96 × 10 = 18 ± 19.6 minutes, or about −1.6 to 37.6 minutes per week. The estimate is positive, but the interval includes almost no change and effects above half an hour. If the practical benchmark is 30 minutes per week, the interval crosses it, so the study does not pin down whether that target is reached. This evidence alone does not prove the policy caused exercise changes or that benefits exceed costs. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 7: Inference for Numerical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.
Start with a question, design and null m: Begin by writing the comparison in the units that a reader can audit. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the estimand is the difference in mean monthly spending between two customer groups, measured in US dollars per customer during January 2026. If group A averages $42 and group B $39, the estimated difference is $42 − $39 = $3 per customer per month. A null of zero says the population difference is $0 per customer per month for the defined groups and period; it does not say every customer spends equally. A survey sample may support an association, but it does not by itself show that membership caused spending. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values’ in the linked sources.
Why 0.05 is not a cliff: Treat nearby p-values as a graded evidential difference, then inspect magnitude and precision. Illustrative synthetic example: Study A estimates a wage gain of $0.20 per hour with p = 0.049; Study B estimates $0.21 per hour with p = 0.051. The estimates differ by only $0.01 per hour, and rounding or modest model changes could affect the displayed p-values. Calling A “real” and B “no effect” creates a discontinuity unsupported by those numbers. The dollar amounts are not automatically useful: over 160 work hours, $0.20 per hour corresponds to $0.20 × 160 = $32 per month before taxes, assuming that schedule. Neither p-value proves causality, and neither assesses the worker’s costs or long-run consequences. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wasserstein, Schirm & Lazar (2019) — Moving to a World Beyond p < 0.05’ in the linked sources.
Power, errors and study design: Power is easiest to communicate with a target effect and a probability scale. Illustrative synthetic example: before a survey, researchers define a meaningful improvement of 4 percentage points in the share completing training and plan a design with β = 0.20. Power = 1 − β = 1 − 0.20 = 0.80, or 80%, for detecting that specified 4-point improvement under the planned assumptions. It does not mean an 80% chance that the eventual estimate is correct. If only 60% of sampled people respond, the effective sample may be smaller and power may fall; nonresponse can also introduce bias that more observations do not automatically fix. The 4 percentage points describe a difference in rates, not a 4% relative increase. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 6: Inference for Categorical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.
Multiplicity and the search process: Multiplicity can be shown with a simple probability calculation. Illustrative synthetic example: imagine 20 independent tests, each using a 5% cutoff, while every null hypothesis is actually true. The probability of no false positive is approximately 0.95^20 ≈ 0.358, so the probability of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.358 = 0.642, or about 64.2%. Independence is a simplifying assumption, and dependence can change the number, but searching still matters. If an analyst examines 20 monthly event windows and highlights the one with p = 0.04, that p-value describes the selected window’s calculation, not the whole search process. Disclosure, preregistration, or an appropriate adjustment is needed; the arithmetic does not prove every finding is false. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.
Association, prediction and causality: Separate the unit of prediction from the unit of causal change. Illustrative synthetic example: across 100 synthetic firms, an observational regression finds that each additional 1 percentage point of quarterly sales growth is associated with 0.3 percentage points higher quarterly return. The arithmetic says a 2-point sales-growth difference corresponds to 0.3 × 2 = 0.6 percentage points of fitted return difference, not that changing sales growth would cause a 0.6-point return. Industry conditions could influence both variables, and an average association may predict poorly for a new firm. A causal claim would need a design or assumptions addressing confounding, timing and selection. The units are percentage points of return, not percent probability and not a guaranteed dollar gain. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values’ in the linked sources.
Beyond statistical significance: transpa: A transparent conclusion can be written as a compact audit trail. Illustrative synthetic example: a randomized pilot estimates a reduction of 6 percentage points in missed appointments, with a 95% interval from −11 to −1 percentage points and p = 0.02. Report the outcome unit, follow-up period, assignment rule, missing-data handling and whether this was the pre-specified primary outcome. The interval suggests reductions from 1 to 11 percentage points are compatible with the analysis, while the sign convention must be stated clearly. It does not show that savings exceed programme costs, that the effect persists after six months, or that the result generalizes to other clinics. A reader should also see exploratory outcomes and deviations from plan, rather than only the favorable headline. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.

Start with a question, units and a fitte: Read a fitted line as a compact summary of the sample, not as a rule for every person. Imagine a teaching model for weekly earnings: predicted pay = £300 + £25 × years of schooling. At 12 years the model predicts £300 + 12 × £25 = £600; at 13 years it predicts £625. The slope, £25 per year, is the model’s average difference in predicted pay for a one-year difference in schooling over the data being modelled. The £300 intercept is the model’s predicted value at zero years; if the data contain no such cases, it may be only a mathematical anchor rather than a useful real-world prediction.

The line describes a conditional average, so individual people can earn more or less; their residual is observed pay minus predicted pay. A straight-line summary can miss curves, and predictions far outside the observed schooling range are extrapolations. Most importantly, people with more schooling may also differ in family background, prior opportunity or other factors, so the slope is not automatically the causal payoff to an extra year. Check residuals and the sample range, and use a credible design for causal claims. See the NIST regression references and Angrist & Pischke Chapter 3 linked below.

Before fitting, identify what one row represents and keep the time unit fixed. Suppose a synthetic sample records quarterly household spending in dollars and hours worked per week: a fitted line is spending = 420 dollars + 18 dollars per weekly hour. For a household working 30 hours, the arithmetic is 420 dollars + (18 dollars/hour × 30 hours) = 960 dollars per quarter. Raising hours from 30 to 32 changes the fitted value by 2 × 18 = 36 dollars per quarter, not 36 percent. This is an average comparison within the observed range, assuming the linear summary is reasonable and measurements are comparable. It does not show that adding work hours causes spending to rise; income, household size, and other factors may differ. For an introduction to fitting and interpreting a linear regression, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 8: Introduction to Linear Regression’ in the linked sources.
Calculate residuals and read what they l: Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data; monthly units): suppose a simple model uses a town’s average bus fare in January, February and March to predict monthly passenger trips per 1,000 residents. The fitted equation is predicted trips = 12,000 − 300 × fare, where fare is measured in pounds per ride and predicted trips are rides per month. In February, the fare is £2.00 and the observed total is 11,600 rides per 1,000 residents. The fitted value is 12,000 − 300(2.00) = 11,400 rides, so the residual is observed minus fitted = 11,600 − 11,400 = +200 rides per 1,000 residents. The positive residual means February had more trips than this line predicts; it does not by itself explain why.

Use residuals to assess what the fitted line leaves behind, not to prove a policy effect. A useful diagnostic is a residual plot against fitted values, fare or calendar month: a curved pattern suggests that a straight line misses nonlinearity, a funnel shape suggests changing variance, and runs across months may indicate dependence. The calculation also assumes the recorded outcome and fare are measured consistently and that the model form is reasonable over the observed fare range. A common mistake is to call a positive residual a causal impact of cheaper transport; it is only an observed-minus-predicted difference under this model. For diagnostic guidance, see “NIST — Residual Diagnostics” in the linked sources below.

A residual can be compared across cases only when its outcome units are clear. Consider synthetic weekly forecasts of electricity demand in megawatt-hours (MWh): the model predicts 1,250 MWh for week 6, while actual recorded demand is 1,310 MWh. Thus e = 1,310 MWh − 1,250 MWh = +60 MWh, meaning demand exceeded the fitted value by 60 MWh. If another week has a −60 MWh residual, the magnitudes match but the signs show opposite errors. Plotting these residuals in calendar order can reveal a pattern: four positive errors in a row may indicate an omitted seasonal effect. The calculation assumes the same demand definition and forecast horizon for both numbers. It does not identify the cause of the miss or prove a policy effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Residual Diagnostics’ in the linked sources.
Measure fit without mistaking R-squared: R-squared is dimensionless, so it should not be described as 0.40 dollars or 40 percentage points. With synthetic annual-income data, suppose SST = 500,000,000 dollar-squared and SSE = 350,000,000 dollar-squared. Then R² = 1 − 350,000,000/500,000,000 = 1 − 0.70 = 0.30, or 30 percent. The model explains 30 percent of the in-sample squared variation around the sample mean under this calculation; the remaining 70 percent is not a claim that each person is predicted 70 percent incorrectly. A second model might reach R² = 0.35 yet make worse future predictions if it overfits. Interpretation assumes the sums use the same sample and outcome scale. R-squared does not establish causal impact, unbiased forecasts, or practical value. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 8: Introduction to Linear Regression (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.
Separate mean-response uncertainty from: Use the interval type that matches the decision. Suppose synthetic data give a fitted mean monthly revenue of 80,000 dollars for stores receiving 10 advertisements, with a 95% confidence interval of 78,000–82,000 dollars. This concerns the average revenue for comparable stores at that advertising level. A 95% prediction interval of 60,000–100,000 dollars concerns one new store and is wider because store-specific variation is included. The midpoint is 80,000 dollars; its half-width is 20,000 dollars, versus 2,000 dollars for the mean interval. These dollar units refer to one month, not an annual total. The interpretation assumes a suitable model, representative sampling, and stable conditions; 95% does not mean this interval has a 95% chance after calculation. Neither interval proves advertising causes revenue. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 501 — Regression Inference and Prediction Intervals (Lesson 7)’ in the linked sources.
Validate predictions on data the model d: For a time-ordered test, calculate errors using only information available before each forecast. Suppose three synthetic test-month sales outcomes are 100, 120, and 80 units, while predictions are 90, 130, and 70 units. Absolute errors are |100−90| = 10, |120−130| = 10, and |80−70| = 10 units, so MAE = (10 + 10 + 10)/3 = 10 units per month. A random split could accidentally let a later market regime influence training, making this score look safer than a chronological test. The metric is on the outcome scale, so it is not 10 percent unless the outcome itself is defined as a percent. This comparison assumes test outcomes are measured consistently. Low MAE shows predictive performance in that test setting, not causality or guaranteed future accuracy. For residual diagnostics and validation practice, see ‘NIST — Residual Diagnostics’ in the linked sources.
Association, prediction and causality in: In a synthetic example, a fund’s monthly excess return is 1 percentage point when the market’s excess return is 2 percentage points, and the fitted intercept is 0 percentage points with beta 0.8 fund percentage points per market percentage point. The fitted fund return is 0 + 0.8 × 2 = 1.6 percentage points, so the residual is 1.0 − 1.6 = −0.6 percentage points. The negative residual is a model error for that month, not a loss caused by the market. Beta summarizes average association over the chosen sample and may change with fees, exposures, or regimes. It does not say that forcing the market up by 1 percentage point would cause the fund to rise 0.8 points. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §§3.1–3.2.3’ in the linked sources.
Conditional averages are not automatical: A conditional average compares observations that share predictor values; it does not automatically construct a counterfactual. Suppose a synthetic wage model compares workers with and without training while controlling for age. The fitted conditional mean is 24 dollars per hour for trained workers and 21 dollars per hour for comparable untrained workers, a difference of 24 − 21 = 3 dollars per hour. The figure is an association in hourly wage units. Motivated workers may seek training, leaving motivation as an omitted factor, so the 3-dollar difference need not be the causal effect of training. Conditioning on a post-training variable could remove part of an effect. Causal interpretation requires assumptions about selection and timing; fit alone is insufficient. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 05: Linear Regression (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

Association is not the missing counterfa: A useful way to see the problem is to imagine a job-training programme. In an illustrative record, people who attended later earn £25,000 on average and people who did not attend earn £22,000, a raw gap of £3,000. That is a real difference between the observed groups, but it is not yet the programme effect. People who chose training may already have had more time, support or motivation. For each trainee, the key missing comparison is what that same person would have earned at the same time without training.

Causal inference defines the target first—for example, the average effect of offering training to eligible jobseekers—then asks which design can estimate the missing alternative. Random assignment, a policy threshold or a defensible comparison over time can help, but each relies on different assumptions and may answer a different population-level question. A regression adjustment cannot prove those assumptions just by including many variables. The Penn State notes on bias and confounding and the World Bank DIME causal-inference materials linked below give more examples.

An association can persist even when the proposed treatment has no effect. Illustrative synthetic example: among 500 customers, 150 who use a budgeting app save £40 per month, while 350 non-users save £30 per month. The observed difference is £40 − £30 = £10 per month. That £10 is a group contrast, not the amount the same users would have saved without the app. Suppose app users were already saving £8 more per month before download; a simple before-treatment comparison would leave only £2 per month as a rough residual, though changing prices or habits could still matter. The comparison requires a credible design and a defined month. It does not establish causation or persistence. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 507 — Bias and Confounding’ in the linked sources.
Potential outcomes and treatment effects: Consider a council deciding whether to offer jobseekers a travel-supported training place. For applicant i, Yᵢ(1) records whether they would be in paid work three months later if offered a place, while Yᵢ(0) records the same applicant’s outcome without the offer. The individual effect Yᵢ(1) − Yᵢ(0) is either −1, 0 or +1 for this binary outcome, but only one potential outcome is observed. A randomized offer can estimate an average effect for the eligible group; it cannot reveal both outcomes for each person. This is a constructed example, not programme data. See Matheus Facure’s Chapter 02, “Randomised Experiments,” in the linked sources below.

Potential outcomes clarify why an average treatment effect is a population summary rather than a personal guarantee. Illustrative synthetic example: 80 applicants are randomly offered coaching and 80 are not. After six months, 28 offered applicants and 20 controls are employed. The offer-group rate is 28/80 = 35%, and the control rate is 20/80 = 25%, so the estimated intention-to-treat effect is 35% − 25% = 10 percentage points. Some may gain, remain unchanged, or be harmed; the group average does not reveal which person belongs to which category. Randomization supports the comparison if assignment is followed and outcomes are measured consistently. It does not reveal both potential outcomes for any applicant or guarantee this 10-point effect elsewhere. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 02: Randomised Experiments (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.
DAGs: confounders, mediators and collide: In an illustrative apprenticeship study, prior work experience may affect both enrolment and later earnings, making it a plausible confounder. A current job type could instead sit on the pathway from training to earnings; controlling for it would remove part of the total effect. Restricting the sample to applicants who received an interview can also be risky if both training and unmeasured motivation affect interview receipt: selection on that shared consequence may create a misleading association. Draw the assumed arrows before choosing controls, and state whether the target is a total or direct effect. These pathways are hypotheses for a design, not empirical findings. See Matheus Facure’s Chapter 04, “Graphical Causal Models,” in the linked sources below.

A DAG helps distinguish a variable worth adjusting for from one that creates bias when conditioned on. Illustrative synthetic example: among customers with matched account age, 60% offered coaching open a savings account, compared with 50% not offered. If prior financial literacy raises both the chance of receiving coaching and account opening, literacy is a confounder; adjusting for it may make the comparison more credible. If coaching first increases a savings plan, that plan is a mediator, so controlling for it would remove part of the total coaching effect. If analysts keep only customers approved for a loan, and both coaching and income affect approval, approval is a collider. That 10-point gap need not be causal. These are hypothetical pathways, not observed facts; timing and measurement must support the graph. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Harvard — Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs’ in the linked sources.
Difference-in-differences and thresholds: Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data; weekly employment rate, measured in percentage points over two quarters): suppose a town introduces a subsidized bus pass in Quarter 2 for Northside residents, while similar Southside remains a comparison area. Northside employment is 54% in Q1 and 60% in Q2, a +6 percentage-point change. Southside is 52% and 55%, a +3-point change. Difference-in-differences = (60−54)−(55−52) = 6−3 = 3 percentage points. The estimate says Northside employment improved 3 points more than the comparison area after the subsidy, under the design assumptions. The Q2 gap is 5 points (60−55), but that is not the DiD; Northside’s own 6-point increase also includes changes shared by both areas.

Difference-in-differences can identify an average policy effect when the comparison group provides a credible counterfactual trend; it cannot by itself prove that the subsidy caused the entire post-period difference or that every resident benefited. The key check is parallel trends: inspect several pre-policy quarters and plot both areas, looking for similar movements before Q2; a placebo policy date can provide an additional diagnostic. Watch for spillovers, such as Southside residents using the passes, or different employment measurement across areas. A common mistake is to call Northside’s 6-point before-to-after rise the treatment effect, ignoring the comparison change. See “World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods” in the linked sources below.

A threshold design identifies a local comparison, not automatically a policy effect for everyone. Illustrative synthetic example: a grant is offered to firms scoring at least 70 on an eligibility index. Firms just below the cutoff have a 52% three-month adoption rate, while firms just above have 59%; the jump is 59% − 52% = 7 percentage points. Because the groups are close to 70, the comparison can be credible if firms cannot precisely manipulate scores and other determinants change smoothly at the cutoff. The 7-point estimate applies near score 70, for this grant and three-month period; it need not apply to firms scoring 40 or 95. A small sample or a narrow score window can also make the estimate imprecise. For a fuller treatment, see ‘World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods’ in the linked sources.
Randomized experiments and implementatio: Implementation determines whether an experiment estimates an offer effect or an effect of actually receiving treatment. Synthetic example: 300 customers per arm are assigned a budgeting webinar. In the offer arm, 210 attend; enrollment is 27% among all 300 offered customers, versus 22% among 300 controls. The intention-to-treat estimate is 27% − 22% = 5 percentage points. Dividing 5 points by the 70% attendance rate gives about 7.14 points, but that is not automatically a valid treatment-on-the-treated effect: non-attenders may differ from attenders, and assignment can affect behavior even without attendance. Assume assignment is random, outcomes are recorded for all 600 customers, and contamination is limited. The result concerns offering one webinar over the stated follow-up period, not guaranteed long-run enrollment. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 02: Randomised Experiments (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.
Instrumental variables, uncertainty and: An instrumental variable can estimate an effect for compliers when its assumptions are plausible, but the arithmetic and target must be stated carefully. Illustrative synthetic example: an encouragement is randomly sent to 200 customers; 40 adopt a savings plan, versus 20 of 200 not encouraged. Adoption rises 40/200 − 20/200 = 20% − 10% = 10 percentage points. Average monthly deposits rise from £18 to £20, a difference of £2 per month. The Wald estimate is £2 ÷ 0.10 = £20 per month per full-unit adoption effect, interpreted for compliers under the model. This requires relevance, independence, and no direct effect of encouragement on deposits except through adoption. It does not prove a £20 increase for every customer or transport to another product, month, or population. For a fuller treatment, see ‘World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods’ in the linked sources.

Estimate the effect of the offer first: Keep the lottery groups intact when you calculate the first result. Suppose 100 eligible jobseekers are randomly offered a course and 100 are not; 80 of the offered group attend, while 20 people in the comparison group find similar training elsewhere. If employment one year later is 72% in the offer group and 66% in the comparison group, the intention-to-treat effect is 72% − 66% = 6 percentage points. It answers the practical question, “What was the effect of offering this programme under the take-up we actually achieved?”

Do not instead compare the 80 attendees with everyone else: attendance is no longer randomized. The 6-point offer effect is also not automatically the effect of attending. Under extra instrumental-variable assumptions, dividing 6 points by the 60-point difference in take-up (80% − 20%) gives a 10-point effect for people whose participation changed because of the offer—not necessarily for every participant. Differential missing follow-up or spillovers can still undermine the comparison. See the experimental-ideal chapters linked below for the distinction between assignment and receipt.

The intention-to-treat calculation remains useful when the programme is inconvenient or alternatives exist. In an illustrative synthetic trial, 150 households are offered an energy-saving visit and 150 are not. After three months, average electricity use is 420 kilowatt-hours per household in the offer group and 450 kilowatt-hours in control. The ITT contrast is 420 − 450 = −30 kilowatt-hours per household over three months: the offer reduced use by 30 kilowatt-hours on average, under the observed take-up pattern. It is not the saving among visitors alone, because visits were not randomly received. Nor does it establish effects in winter if this trial ran in summer. For a fuller treatment, see “Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)” in the linked sources.
Random assignment builds a comparison: Illustrative synthetic example: a city randomly assigns 200 unemployed adults to an offer group or a comparison group, 100 in each, for a six-month childcare-subsidy pilot. The offer group can claim a subsidy, while the comparison group receives no pilot offer during those six months. At month 6, average weekly earnings are £310 for the offer group and £280 for the comparison group. The assignment contrast is £310 − £280 = £30 per person per week. Interpreted carefully, the randomized offer is associated with an average increase of £30 in weekly earnings over six months, compared with what the offer group would have experienced on average without the offer. This calculation uses original assignment, not who actually claimed the subsidy.

Random assignment can support this average causal comparison, but it cannot prove that every individual gained £30, reveal each person’s unobserved alternative outcome, or guarantee the result applies to all unemployed adults or a later year. Check that assignment probabilities were followed and compare pre-offer characteristics across groups; noticeable imbalances can occur by chance in one sample, so a balance table is a diagnostic rather than proof of success. Also check missing month-6 earnings and possible sharing of subsidy information across groups. Do not misinterpret the £30 as the effect for subsidy claimants only: selective take-up changes that question. For a fuller treatment, see “Matheus Facure — Ch. 02: Randomised Experiments (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)” in the linked sources below.

Random assignment is easiest to picture as a lottery performed before outcomes occur. Suppose 120 tenants are assigned equally to a reminder letter about rent support or to no letter: 60 per group. Six months later, 45 offered tenants and 36 comparison tenants are current on rent. The rates are 45/60 = 75% and 36/60 = 60%, so the assignment contrast is 15 percentage points, not 15 percent. These illustrative, synthetic counts estimate the average effect of being offered the reminder in this eligible sample. A different random draw could produce a different gap, and the result does not show that every tenant benefited or that the letter caused the same change elsewhere. For a fuller treatment, see “Angrist & Pischke — Mastering ’Metrics (Princeton University Press)” in the linked sources.
Non-compliance changes the estimand: Non-compliance creates distinct groups: compliers, always-takers, never-takers, and possibly defiers. Consider an illustrative synthetic trial of 200 people: 100 are offered counselling, with 70 attending; 100 are controls, with 20 obtaining counselling elsewhere. Attendance therefore differs by 70% − 20% = 50 percentage points. If employment is 64% among those offered and 54% among controls, the ITT is 10 percentage points. Under exclusion, a genuine first stage, and monotonicity, 10 ÷ 0.50 = 20 percentage points is a Wald estimate for compliers, not for all attendees or everyone eligible. The arithmetic uses proportions on a 0–1 scale after converting percentage points to 0.50. These assumptions may fail if the offer changes outcomes through another channel. For a fuller treatment, see “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 2, §§2.2–2.3” in the linked sources.
Audit what happened after assignment: An audit should compare both missingness and exposure, not merely the final averages. In an illustrative synthetic trial, 240 people are assigned equally: 120 offer and 120 control. Follow-up is missing for 12 offered people and 6 controls, so missingness is 12/120 = 10% versus 6/120 = 5%, a five-percentage-point difference. If the observed outcome averages are 8.4 and 7.9 points, the apparent contrast is 0.5 test-score points, but unequal loss could make it misleading. Also record whether control members received the programme from friends or providers; such spillovers dilute the offer contrast. These checks do not prove what missing outcomes would have been or guarantee transfer to another district. For a fuller treatment, see “Edward Rubin — EC 607: Lecture 02: The Experimental Ideal (license not stated; link only)” in the linked sources.
Use pre-treatment measures for precision: A baseline measure can make a noisy follow-up comparison more precise without changing the assignment question. In an illustrative synthetic tutoring trial, offered pupils start at 50 points on average and controls at 49; after eight weeks, their averages are 62 and 59. The unadjusted difference is 62 − 59 = 3 points. If baseline scores predict follow-up scores, analysts can compare outcomes after accounting for those pre-offer scores, while still reporting the assignment contrast. By contrast, attendance is measured after assignment: if the offer raises attendance from 60% to 80%, selecting only attendees compares selected people, not lottery groups. Baseline adjustment cannot prove the tutoring caused every point of the gap, and post-treatment controls need a separate causal argument. For a fuller treatment, see “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)” in the linked sources.

The Wald ratio shows whose effect an ins: Follow the ratio one piece at a time. Suppose a randomly assigned offer increases programme participation by 0.20, or 20 percentage points, and increases average annual earnings by £300. The reduced-form change in earnings is £300 per eligible person; the first-stage change in participation is 0.20. Dividing £300 by 0.20 gives £1,500 per additional participant induced by the offer. The denominator rescales the effect of being offered access into an effect per unit of participation; if the first stage were only 0.02, the same £300 reduced form would imply a much larger and less stable £15,000 ratio.

That calculation is causal only if the offer is relevant, as-if randomly assigned for the comparison, affects earnings only through participation, and does not make some people participate less while making others participate more under the standard complier interpretation. The estimate then describes people whose take-up responds to the instrument, not automatically every eligible person. A strong first stage cannot prove the exclusion assumption, and a weak one makes uncertainty fragile. See Angrist & Pischke Chapter 4 and the open Mixtape text linked below.

Monotonicity helps give the Wald ratio a complier interpretation: the instrument encourages some people and does not discourage others. Illustrative synthetic example: a randomly assigned reminder increases vaccination from 60% to 70%, a 0.10 probability increase, and raises average preventive-care visits by 0.30 visits per person during the following 12 months. The ratio is 0.30 ÷ 0.10 = 3.0 additional visits per induced vaccination. Here visits are measured in visits per person per year, while 0.10 is a probability difference; dividing gives visits per vaccinated complier, not visits per percentage point. The estimate need not apply to people who would vaccinate regardless of the reminder or never vaccinate. It also requires no direct reminder effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 09: Non-compliance and LATE (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.
Read two-stage least squares: Illustrative synthetic example (annual earnings, January–December 2025): A city randomly offers eligible jobseekers a free place in a skills course, but some offered people do not attend and some unoffered people find another course. Let Z be the offer, D be course attendance (0 or 1), and Y be earnings during 2025, measured in pounds. The offer raises attendance from 30% to 50%, so the first-stage change is 0.20. Average earnings are £18,000 for the unoffered group and £18,240 for the offered group, so the reduced-form change is £240 per eligible person. In a simple two-stage calculation, 2SLS divides £240 by 0.20, giving £1,200 in annual earnings per additional participant induced by the offer. Stage 1 isolates offer-driven attendance; stage 2 uses that predicted attendance to estimate its outcome relationship.

2SLS can identify the effect of attendance for the people whose attendance changes because of the offer, but it cannot automatically establish the effect for every jobseeker or prove that the course caused all observed earnings differences. Check that the first stage is sufficiently strong and report its estimate and uncertainty; a tiny attendance change makes the ratio unstable. Also defend independence, exclusion, and the relevant design assumptions: the offer should not affect 2025 earnings through another route, such as a separate cash benefit. A common mistake is to read £1,200 as the average return to attending for everyone; it is a local effect for induced participants under the assumptions. Angrist & Pischke — Mostly Harmless Econometrics (Princeton University Press) explains the framework in the linked sources below.

Think of 2SLS as replacing observed treatment with the part predicted by the instrument. Illustrative synthetic example: a permit lottery changes business participation from 0.30 to 0.45, so predicted participation rises by 0.15 (15 percentage points). Average quarterly revenue rises from $8,000 to $8,600, a reduced-form increase of $600 per eligible business per quarter. The just-identified ratio is $600 ÷ 0.15 = $4,000 of quarterly revenue per additional participant induced by the lottery. Stage 1 supplies the 0.15; stage 2 uses that instrument-predicted participation. The units are dollars per business per quarter, not dollars per percentage point. This interpretation requires independence and exclusion and may describe compliers only; it is not automatically the effect for every business. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Causal Inference: The Mixtape — open first-edition text’ in the linked sources.
Why ordinary regression may fail: A useful diagnostic is to ask whether the unobserved factor differs systematically across treatment levels. Illustrative synthetic numbers: among 100 workers, 50 take a training course and earn £2,400 per month on average; 50 do not and earn £2,000. The raw gap is £400 per month, but suppose the trainees would have earned £300 more even without training because they had greater prior motivation. A simple regression that omits motivation can therefore attribute part of £400 to training. An instrument aims to create treatment differences unrelated to that omitted motivation. This example does not show that training has no effect; it shows why association alone cannot separate effects. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’ in the linked sources.
Three conditions shape the argument: The three conditions can be checked as separate questions rather than treated as one test. Illustrative synthetic example: a lottery offer (Z) raises course enrollment (D) from 40% to 55%, a 15 percentage-point first-stage increase. That supports relevance, but suppose the lottery also gives winners a £100 cash voucher. The voucher could raise monthly spending directly, so exclusion is doubtful even with a clear 15 percentage-point change. Independence would additionally require comparable lottery groups, perhaps after pre-specified controls; a chance imbalance in baseline income can threaten that story. Percentages here are probabilities on a 0–1 or percentage scale, not currency amounts. Regression output cannot establish the institutional claim that no direct path exists. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke — Mastering ’Metrics (Princeton University Press)’ in the linked sources.
Check strength and scope: Strength and scope require looking beyond one coefficient. Illustrative synthetic first-stage results from a sample of 500 applicants show participation of 52% for instrument-exposed applicants and 50% for others: the difference is 0.02, or 2 percentage points. If the reduced-form outcome difference is $180 in annual income per applicant, the ratio is $180 ÷ 0.02 = $9,000 per induced participant per year. That large-looking number may be sensitive to sampling noise because only a small share changes treatment. Also ask whose participation moved: applicants near an eligibility threshold may not represent all applicants. A first-stage statistic addresses relevance, not whether the instrument is independent or excluded. Report units, uncertainty, and design-specific diagnostics; do not generalize a local estimate without justification. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data (MIT Press)’ in the linked sources.
Weak instruments make conventional inter: A small denominator magnifies ordinary measurement noise. Illustrative synthetic numbers: an instrument changes treatment probability by 0.01, or 1 percentage point, while the estimated outcome change is $50 per person per year. The Wald ratio is $50 ÷ 0.01 = $5,000 per induced treatment per year. If sampling error changes the reduced form by only $20, the ratio becomes $70 ÷ 0.01 = $7,000; if it changes it to $30, the ratio becomes $3,000. The $4,000 swing comes from modest outcome noise, not a new economic mechanism. These are synthetic figures, not historical observations. Weakness concerns relevance and inference; it does not repair independence or exclusion. Report the first stage and use suitable robust procedures rather than trusting an ordinary interval automatically. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 4, §§4.1–4.6’ in the linked sources.

Calculate the contrast before reading a: Use four group averages and keep each subtraction visible. Suppose employment in the treated region rises from 50% before a policy to 56% after it: a 6-percentage-point change. In a comparison region it rises from 48% to 51%: a 3-point change. Difference-in-differences is 6 − 3 = 3 percentage points. The comparison change removes the 3-point improvement the treated region might have shared because of the wider economy. The post-period gap is 5 points and the treated region’s own change is 6 points; neither is the DiD contrast.

The causal interpretation needs the treated region’s average outcome, without the policy, to have followed the comparison region’s trend over this period. Several pre-policy observations can reveal some warning signs, but a flat-looking pre-trend cannot prove the unobserved post-policy path. Anticipation, spillovers, changing group composition or different outcome measurement can also break the comparison. When policies start at different times and effects vary, a familiar two-way fixed-effects regression may combine unintended comparisons. See Angrist & Pischke Chapter 5 and the open DiD materials linked below.

Before interpreting a coefficient, reproduce its intended two-by-two contrast from group means and record the measurement unit. Illustrative synthetic example: monthly electricity use falls from 900 to 840 kilowatt-hours in a treated building, a change of −60 kWh. A comparison building falls from 760 to 730 kWh, a change of −30 kWh. Thus DiD = (840 − 900) − (730 − 760) = −60 − (−30) = −30 kWh per building-month. The treated building declined 30 kWh more than the comparison, but this is causal only if the comparison captures its no-policy change and measurement, occupancy, and timing are comparable. The result does not say every building saved 30 kWh or that the policy caused the decline without those assumptions. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)’ in the linked sources.
Use event time with care: Illustrative synthetic example: A county introduces a childcare subsidy in April 2025, and a similar county does not. The outcome is the monthly employment rate, measured in percentage points; April is event month 0, and March (event month −1) is the omitted baseline. Relative to that baseline, the treated-minus-comparison gap is −0.2 points in February (−2), 0.4 points in May (+1), and 1.5 points in June (+2). The June estimate can be read transparently: the treated county’s rate rose 2.0 points from March to June while the comparison county’s rate rose 0.5 points, so 2.0 − 0.5 = 1.5 percentage points. The sequence suggests when the gap appeared, rather than only reporting one before–after number.

An event-study pattern can describe timing and is useful for checking whether pre-treatment differences look compatible with a common trend, but it cannot by itself establish that the subsidy caused the later employment change. The key decision check is to inspect several pre-policy event-time estimates, their uncertainty, and whether the counties experienced spillovers, other policies, or composition changes; also state the omitted month and outcome definition. A common misinterpretation is to treat pre-period coefficients near zero as proof that parallel trends will hold after treatment: they are diagnostics, not proof of an unobserved counterfactual. Effects may also vary with adoption timing. For further guidance, see “Matheus Facure — Ch. 13: Difference-in-Differences (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)” in the linked sources below.

Event time labels observations by distance from treatment, making timing easier to compare than calendar dates alone. Illustrative synthetic example: a benefit begins in quarter 0. Relative to quarter −1, the treated-minus-comparison outcome gap is −0.3 percentage points at −2, 0.1 points at 0, and 1.2 points at +2. The post-treatment change in the gap from −1 to +2 is 1.2 − 0.0 = 1.2 percentage points, while the −2 estimate is a pre-treatment diagnostic. These values describe when differences appear; they do not establish causality, because anticipation, other shocks, or selective composition could create the pattern. A graph should show confidence intervals, the omitted reference period, and the outcome’s unit. Testing many leads also creates opportunities for chance findings. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 13: Difference-in-Differences (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.
Take a difference in each group: A useful way to organize the calculation is to write each group’s change with its units before subtracting. Illustrative synthetic example: a training program is offered in Store A, where weekly sales rise from $1,200 before to $1,350 after, a $150 increase. In Store B, sales rise from $1,100 to $1,180, an $80 increase. The DiD contrast is $150 − $80 = $70 per store-week. This says Store A improved by $70 per week more than Store B over the comparison, not that the program definitely caused $70; that interpretation needs a credible untreated trend and no differential shocks. Stable level differences, such as Store A’s initially higher sales, are removed, but changing customer mix may remain. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke — Mastering ’Metrics (Princeton University Press)’ in the linked sources.
